accelerator_load.method: load the persisted accelerator for the committed root, binary container vs. legacy JSON envelope, mean over repeated loads

build_profile: debug (unoptimized) unless built with --release; absolute times are host/build dependent, byte counts are exact

historical_root_open.method: Snapshot::open_dir for distinct roots of a small-payload history: cold (no accelerator) replays from a checkpoint; warm loads the persisted accelerator. The discovery directory is already complete, so cold opens differ only by the accelerator.

mount_quick_open.method: checkpoint::open_index_quick loads a validated accelerator for exactly the committed root: a quick open (log not replayed), never an audit. Compare against the catalogue-assisted audited mount on the same volume.

mount_recovery.method: mount_index cold completes a scan and publishes the derived committed-root directory; mount_index warm consults it and skips the whole-log discovery scan; mount_index_scan is the pre-Phase-43 algorithm (always scans)

note: This file measures where Phase 43 does and does not help, honestly. (1) The binary accelerator replaces a large JSON envelope with a small validated header plus packed inode/directory tables, so a *warm* historical-root open (and a validated quick open) parses fewer bytes and allocates less; a *cold* open is largely unchanged because it is dominated by the log reconstruction, not by the accelerator. (2) The committed-root directory lets a warm restart skip the whole-log checkpoint discovery scan, but the checkpoint's embedded index must still be decoded, and a mount with no usable checkpoint still replays the whole log. The directory and every accelerator are derived state: a corrupt, torn, truncated, foreign, or missing one always falls back to the authoritative reconstruction. Allocation and page-fault figures are process-global deltas and may be perturbed by concurrently running tests.
